summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted for worsening right leg pain and ulcers, found to be due to calciphylaxis and severe peripheral arterial disease. She had markedly elevated PTH, leading to a parathyroidectomy, after which she developed hungry bone syndrome with symptomatic hypocalcemia requiring IV calcium replacement and close monitoring. A CT angiogram revealed critical stenosis in the right femoral artery, prompting angioplasty and stenting, complicated by distal embolization and persistent foot ischemia. Despite interventions, her right foot remained cool, dusky, and painful, with vascular surgery deferring amputation pending demarcation. Calciphylaxis lesions were managed with intralesional sodium thiosulfate after IV therapy was halted due to worsening hypocalcemia. Pain was controlled with a multimodal regimen, and anticoagulation was optimized for her mechanical valve. She was discharged to extended care with plans for ongoing wound care, calcium monitoring, and outpatient follow-up with vascular and dermatology teams.
